trllanes-and-the-troll-house-party:
The settlement of Trøllanes on Kalsoy Island takes its name from ancient trolls who would come ashore once a year to wreak havoc — eating all available food, drinking, dancing, and behaving like wild party-goers. The name itself means 'Troll Ness' or 'Troll Peninsula,' and the settlers who chose to live there centuries ago must have known the reputation of the place. The village sits at the end of a long, narrow valley, sheltered by towering cliffs that funnel the wind into eerie howls — a sound that the old people said was the trolls laughing.

Terrified villagers would flee to Mikladalur every year, leaving their homes to be ransacked. They took what they could carry — food stores, precious tools, children — and retreated to the safety of the neighboring village, locking doors and shuttering windows behind them. But locks and shutters meant nothing to trolls. By morning, the houses were wrecked, the food was gone, and the trolls had moved on, leaving only footprints the size of boats pressed into the mud.

One year, a woman was unable to escape and hid under a table as the trolls danced and feasted above her. The floor shook. The dishes rattled. The trolls sang in voices like grinding stone and laughed with mouths full of food. She could smell them — a sharp, animal scent of wet fur and old earth. In terror, she exclaimed 'Christ!' The trolls, hearing the holy name, fled from the village in panic and never returned. The holy name was their undoing, and Trøllanes was freed. The route to the Kallur lighthouse begins in Trøllanes, offering some of the most dramatic views in the Faroe Islands — a landscape that still feels like troll country.
trllkonufingur-the-troll-womans-finger:
A giant troll-woman from Iceland came to Vágar Island with the same plan as Risin and Kellingin: to steal the Faroe Islands and drag them to Iceland. She crossed the sea at night, swimming through water so cold it would kill a human in minutes, her massive body cutting through the waves like a ship's hull. Like the giants, she could only work at night — sunlight was her enemy, the one force that could undo her plans.

She reached Vágar Island and began to search for a rope strong enough to bind the islands together. But she moved too slowly. The work was harder than she expected, the islands heavier than they looked. She searched the cliffs for the right binding point, her fingers scraping the rock, leaving grooves that can still be seen today.

Caught by sunrise, sunlight turned her to stone. She toppled from the cliff into the sea — and was so enormous that her head became the island of Koltur, while one finger remained above water as the rock formation Trøllkonufingur near Sandavágur. The finger stands like a jagged monument, pointing accusingly at the sky that betrayed her.

Koltur is inhabited by only two people, Bjørn and Lukka Patursson, who live in the shadow of a petrified giantess. The rock formation is visible from the airport, and it is a popular climbing spot — though climbing it is not for the faint-hearted. In 1844, a member of the Royal Danish entourage climbed it, descended, realized he had dropped a glove, climbed back up — and was never seen again. Some say the troll-woman's spirit still guards her finger, punishing those who dare to scale it.
trur-rami-and-the-three-gifts-of-mykines:
A giant named Tórur Rami tried to conquer the island of Mykines. He was a brute of a thing — taller than the sea stacks, with hands like boulders and a voice that shook the cliffs when he spoke. The native inhabitant Óli Rami opposed him, though he was no giant. What Óli Rami lacked in size he made up for in cunning and magic, gifts passed down through generations of island dwellers who had learned to survive in a land of storms and stone.

When the giant approached, Óli Rami used magic to split Mykineshólmur from the main island, creating the islet now reached by a narrow metal bridge. The sea rushed in to fill the gap, and the giant was stranded on the opposite shore, howling with rage. But he was not finished. He jumped across the gap — a leap that would kill any human — and they fought.

Óli Rami won and spared the giant's life in exchange for three gifts: a great whale would appear annually in Hvalagjógv bay — but the people complained about the smell and it stopped; a giant magical tree — but the people complained it was shabby and it withered; gannets that still nest only on Mykineshólmur, their white bodies covering the cliffs like snow. The condition was that the people must never complain about the gifts.

The gannets remain. The whale and the tree are gone, lost to human ingratitude. The lesson of Mykines is simple: the world offers wonders, but only if you accept them without complaint.
grmur-kamban-the-first-settler:
Grímur Kamban is recorded in the Færeyinga Saga as the first Scandinavian settler in the Faroe Islands, arriving around 825 AD — decades before the main Norse colonization of Iceland. He settled at Funningur on Eysturoy, in a narrow valley where the mountains press close to the sea and the wind comes down from the heights like a living thing. The name 'Kamban' may be of Gaelic origin, suggesting he was a Norse-Gael from the British Isles — perhaps from the Hebrides or Ireland, where Norse and Celtic cultures had already begun to merge.

According to legend, he was a feared Viking who fled Norway after committing murder. The story goes that he killed a man in a dispute over land — or was it a woman? — and was exiled rather than executed, his ship pointed toward the western horizon and his fate left to the sea. He found the Faroe Islands and never left.

His settlement at Funningur marks the beginning of continuous habitation in the Faroes. The Færeyinga Saga describes how subsequent settlers arrived and found Grímur already established, his farm carved out of the wilderness, his livestock grazing on the hillside. He was the first, but he would not be the last. The story bridges history and folklore, representing the arrival of humans into a landscape already inhabited by trolls, giants, and hidden people — beings who had claimed the islands long before any human set foot on them.
trndur--gtu-trndur-the-viking-chieftain:
Tróndur í Gøtu was a powerful 10th-century Viking chieftain who lived in Gøta on Eysturoy, in a longhouse overlooking the narrow sound where the sea rushes in at high tide. He is the central figure in the Færeyinga Saga, which recounts his fierce opposition to the Christianization of the islands — a struggle that was as much about political power as it was about faith.

He led pagan resistance against Sigmundur Brestisson, who was sent by King Olaf Tryggvason of Norway to convert the Faroese by force. Tróndur refused. He had served the old gods all his life — Thor, Odin, Freyja — and he would not abandon them for a foreign god brought by foreign warriors. The battles between Tróndur and Sigmundur were fierce, fought across the islands in the long summer months when the sea was calm enough to travel.

After a series of battles, Sigmundur ultimately won and killed Tróndur. But in folklore, Tróndur is often portrayed as a tragic hero — a symbol of Faroese independence and resistance against foreign domination. His burial mound is said to exist near Gøta, a low, grass-covered hill that locals still avoid at night. Some say his ghost walks the shore, still guarding the islands he refused to surrender.
smun-of-kirkjubur-hulda-smun-and-the-hid:
Símun Símunarson, nicknamed Hulda-Símun or Troll-Símun, was a massive farmer at Kirkjubøur on Streymoy — the largest settlement in the Faroe Islands and home to the legendary Magnus Cathedral. He was so large that his jacket required three lengths of double-width cloth, and none of his farmhands dared walk ahead of him on sheep round-ups. He moved through the world like a force of nature, and the world moved out of his way.

A hulduman — a hidden woman — lived on Kirkjubøur Felltop, in the rocky heights above the village where the mist clings to the grass and the wind never stops. The legend tells how Símun was kidnapped by the Huldufólk and taken to the cliffs near Kirkjubøur, spirited away in the night by beings who had lived in the landscape since before humans arrived.

After his encounter with the Hidden People, the Huldufólk were never seen in the village again. Símun returned changed — quieter, more reflective, with a distant look in his eyes that never quite went away. He spoke of what he had seen in the underground world, but the words came slowly, as if the language of the Huldufólk had replaced some of his own. The story reflects Faroese beliefs about the Hidden People dwelling in the landscape and their ability to interact with humans — sometimes kindly, sometimes terribly.
the-troll-who-captured-a-princess:
A classic Faroese folk tale collected by Jakob Jakobsen tells of a troll who lived in a cave high in the mountains and captured a princess to pick lice from his hair. The princess was taken from her father's kingdom — a land of green valleys and stone churches — and carried through the mountains in the troll's massive arms, her screams lost in the wind. She was set to work in the dark cave, picking lice from the troll's tangled hair while he slept.

Three brothers set out to rescue her. The elder two brothers failed — one was tricked by the troll's riddles, the other lost his way in the mountains and was never found. But the youngest — helped by the princess who threw him a ball of yarn to track the cave entrance — confronted the troll. The troll tried to trick the boy but was outwitted, outplayed by a child who had nothing but courage and a length of string.

When the troll gained entry to the king's house by picking the Faroese wooden lock (hvölpalás), the boy killed him. The treacherous brothers claimed credit, but the princess revealed the truth. The youngest brother married the princess and became king. Faroese trolls are creatures of darkness, large and ugly but easily outwitted — a reminder that intelligence and courage matter more than size and strength.
kpakonans-curse-the-seal-womans-revenge:
The darker sequel to the Kópakonan legend. After the seal woman returned to the sea, leaving her human husband Torkil and their children on the shore, Torkil turned his grief into rage. He became a hunter of seals, taking his boat out at dawn and returning at dusk with the bloody carcasses of the creatures he blamed for his loss.

Kópakonan appeared to him in a dream, her face half-seal, half-woman, her eyes dark with grief. 'Do not kill my seal husband and children,' she begged. 'They are my kin as much as you were.' Torkil ignored her warning. The next morning, he went out again.

When he killed her seal family — her new husband, her seal-children, the life she had built in the deep water — Kópakonan rose from the sea. She stood on the shore, her sealskin draped over one arm, her face carved with fury. She pronounced a terrible curse: the men of Mikladalur would die at sea and fall from the cliffs until enough dead men could encircle the entire island of Kalsoy holding hands.

The curse is said to still haunt the village, where the sea claims lives with unusual frequency. The cliffs of Kalsoy are treacherous, and the strait between Kalsoy and Eysturoy is one of the most dangerous in the Faroe Islands. A 2.6-meter bronze statue of Kópakonan by Hans Pauli Olsen stands at the water's edge in Mikladalur since 2014, gazing out to sea where her seal-children swim.
hulduflk-captured-by-a-priest-at-srvgsva:
At Sørvágsvatn Lake on Vágar — the lake that famously appears to hang impossibly over the ocean, suspended on the cliffs like a mirror in the sky — there is a stone mound where, according to legend, a priest trapped several Huldufólk. The priest was a man of iron faith and little patience, who had spent years studying the old texts and the new ones, and who believed that the Hidden People were nothing more than demons in disguise.

The priest used his spiritual authority to imprison the supernatural beings within the mound, speaking prayers in Latin while the Huldufólk wailed and scratched at the stone from inside. He sealed the entrance with a cross carved into the rock, and he walked away, confident that the job was done.

But the job was not done. Visitors to the area claim they can still hear the wailing and cries of the trapped hidden people emanating from the stone, particularly on stormy nights when the wind howls across the lake and the mist rolls in from the ocean. The sounds are faint — more felt than heard — but they are there, a persistent reminder that some things cannot be imprisoned by faith alone.

The legend reflects Faroese beliefs about the power of Christian clergy over pagan supernatural beings, and the common motif of Huldufólk being afraid of crosses, churches, and Christian symbols. It also reflects a deeper truth: that the old ways and the new ways have never fully reconciled, and that the landscape remembers what humans choose to forget.
nykur-and-the-brothers-lake-vatnsdalsvat:
A variant of the Nykur legend told around Lake Vatnsdalsvatn, a body of water so deep that no one has ever measured its bottom. Two children were playing by the lakeshore when they saw a beautiful white horse grazing nearby. Its coat gleamed like fresh snow, its mane flowed like silk, and its eyes were dark and knowing.

The older brother, being tall enough, climbed onto the horse's back. Immediately the horse began galloping toward the deep water. The younger brother, who only wanted his sibling to come back and play, called out his brother's name: 'Jóannes!' The name sounded like the Nykur's true name, and in the Faroe Islands, to speak a water spirit's name is to break its power.

The horse stopped. It stood at the water's edge, trembling, its eyes wild with rage. Then it turned and retreated into the lake, leaving Jóannes standing in the shallows, soaked but alive. The younger brother had saved his sibling with nothing but a name.

The tale serves as a warning to children about the dangers of lakes and the importance of knowing how to counter supernatural threats. Speaking a water spirit's name breaks its spell in Faroese folklore — a piece of knowledge that has saved lives across the centuries. The children of Vatnsdalur still whisper the Nykur's name when they pass the lake, half in fear, half in hope.
draugur-faroese-revenant-legends:
In Faroese folklore, the draugur (dreygur) is a malevolent undead being or revenant, akin to the Norse draugr. Draugar are described as large in build, wearing grey clothes with black hair — the same description given for Huldufólk in Faroese tradition, a detail that has led some scholars to wonder whether the two categories of beings were once the same.

They are said to inhabit graves, mounds, and coastal areas, often guarding treasure or haunting the living. Unlike ghosts, draugar have physical bodies — animated corpses that can swell to enormous size, their fingers curling around the edges of coffins, their eyes glowing in the darkness of churchyards. They smell of death and salt water, and their presence is marked by a cold that seeps into the bones.

In Faroese sea folklore, drowned fishermen may become sea-draugar who haunt the waters where they died. They appear on stormy nights, standing on the waves, their grey clothes flapping in the wind. Sailors who see them know that their ship is doomed. The draugur embodies the thin line between the living and dead in isolated island communities where death at sea was a constant reality — a reality that shaped every aspect of Faroese life, from the songs they sang to the prayers they whispered at dawn.
the-sorceress-of-oyndarfjrur:
The Rinkusteinar legend in its more detailed form. Long ago, when Irish pirates attacked Fuglafjørður, they killed, robbed, and terrorized the village before setting sail for Oyndarfjørður. The pirates came in three ships, their sails black against the grey sky, their oars churning the water into foam. The villagers of Fuglafjørður had already lost everything — their stores, their tools, some of their people — and the pirates were not finished.

An old witch living in Oyndarfjørður saw them coming. She stood on the shore, her hair white as sea foam, her hands raised to the sky. She was old enough to remember the old ways, the magic that had been passed down through generations of women who knew the names of the winds and the secrets of the stone. She raised her arms and cast a powerful curse, transforming the pirate ships into stone.

The two rocking stones are the pirate vessels, forever rocking in the waves near Oyndarfjørður, eternally prevented from reaching their destination. They rock with a motion that seems deliberate, as if the ships are still trying to reach the shore, still trying to complete their mission. The witch's name has been lost to history, but her magic endures. The story is one of the best-known witch legends in the Faroe Islands, a testament to the power of women who defended their communities when no one else could.
faroese-chain-dance-and-kvi-ballad-tradi:
The Faroese chain dance (Føroya Dansur) accompanied by kvæði (ballads) is the national dance and a living tradition that preserves folklore. Dancers form a circle holding hands, moving rhythmically while a kvæðamaður (ballad singer) recites verses recounting tales of legendary heroes, folklore figures, and historical events. The dance moves in a serpentine pattern across the floor, the singers' voices rising and falling with the rhythm of the steps.

Many kvæði date to the Middle Ages and preserve stories otherwise lost, including the Sjúrðar Kvæði (cyclic ballads about Sigurd the Dragon-Slayer from Norse mythology) and ballads about Finnur hin Fróði and other Faroese figures. The ballads are not merely entertainment — they are the living memory of the islands, a repository of history, law, and custom that has been passed down through generations of singers.

The tradition was instrumental in preserving the Faroese language during centuries of Danish rule, when Danish was the official language and Faroese was spoken only in the home. The kvæði kept the old tongue alive, and the chain dance kept the community together. It continues as a living cultural practice at festivals and gatherings, a reminder that the Faroe Islands are not just a place but a people, bound together by song and story.
tippafossur-and-the-killing-of-jgvan:
A grim legend within the Ormur cycle. Jógvan, a farmer from Oyri, caught Ormur of Skála stealing his sheep and attacked him. Miraculously, Jógvan overpowered the huge Ormur and held him down, calling for his son to bring a knife. The scene played out on the hillside above Tippafossur, where the gorge drops away to the sea in a sheer cliff of black basalt.

But the son, terrified of Ormur, fled and hid at the Tippafossur gorge. He could hear his father's shouts echoing across the valley, but he could not move. Ormur's reputation had preceded him — tales of violence and cruelty that had been whispered in every farmhouse on Eysturoy.

Ormur, pinned and fearing death, promised the devil a piece of his little finger in exchange for strength. Suddenly gaining supernatural power, Ormur broke free and killed Jógvan. He then found the boy at Tippafossur and killed him too, the bodies falling into the gorge where the sea could claim them.

Later, in his sleep, Ormur muttered: 'The clothes lie under the corn and the bodies under Tippafossur.' His farmhands heard, found the evidence, and informed the authorities. Ormur was eventually caught, his Achilles' tendon severed by a thrown knife, and executed. He is buried at Stevnuválur overlooking the lands where he committed his crimes — a monument to the darkness that can live in a human heart.
